prompt: Alice and Barbara play a game on a blackboard. At the start, zero is written on the board. Alice goes first, and the players alternate turns. On her turn, each player replaces $x$, the number written on the board, with any real number $y$, subject to the constraint that $0<y-x<1$. The first player to write a number greater than or equal to $2010$ wins. Determine, with proof, who has the winning strategy.

solutions.title: Mirror strategy
solutions.body:
Each move adds a number in $(0,1)$ to the number on the board. Barbara's strategy: whenever Alice adds $z$, Barbara adds $1-z$ (a legal move since $0<1-z<1$). After Barbara's $i$th turn the board shows exactly $i$.

Alice can never write a number $\ge2010$ before Barbara answers: on her $i$th turn the board shows $i-1$ and she writes a number less than $i$, which is below $2010$ for every $i\le2010$. After Alice's $2010$th turn the board shows some $y\in(2009,2010)$, and Barbara writes $2010$ (adding $2010-y<1$) and wins.

**Answer: Barbara has the winning strategy.**

prompt: Alice and Barbara play a game on a blackboard. At the start, zero is written on the board. Alice goes first, and the players alternate turns. On her turn, each player replaces $x$, the number written on the board, with any real number $y$, subject to the constraint that $0<y-x<1$. The first player to write a number greater than or equal to $2010$ on her $2011$th turn or later wins (if a player writes a number greater than or equal to $2010$ on her $2010$th turn or earlier, she loses immediately). Determine, with proof, who has the winning strategy.

solutions.title: Mirror after the first move
solutions.body:
Alice writes any number $a\in(0,1)$ on her first turn and afterwards, whenever Barbara adds $z$, Alice adds $1-z$. After Alice's $i$th turn the board shows $(i-1)+a$.

Barbara never wins first: on her $i$th turn the board shows $(i-1)+a$ and she writes less than $i+a$, which for $i\le2009$ is below $2010$; on her $2010$th turn the board shows $2009+a$ and writing $2010$ or more would make her lose immediately, so she must write some $y\in(2009+a,2010)$. On her $2011$th turn Alice then writes $2010$ (legal, since $2010-y<1$) and wins. (Alice herself never reaches $2010$ early: after her $2010$th turn the board shows $2009+a<2010$.)

**Answer: Alice has the winning strategy.**

prompt: Rachel and Brian are playing a game in a grid with $1$ row of $2011$ squares. Initially, there is one white checker in each of the first two squares from the left, and one black checker in the third square from the left. At each stage, Rachel can choose to either run or fight. If Rachel runs, she moves the black checker $1$ unit to the right, and Brian moves each of the white checkers one unit to the right. If Rachel chooses to fight, she pushes the checker immediately to the left of the black checker $1$ unit to the left, the black checker is moved $1$ unit to the right, and Brian places a new white checker in the cell immediately to the left of the black one. The game ends when the black checker reaches the last cell. How many different final configurations are possible?

solutions.title: Only the number of fights matters
solutions.body:
Both operations move the black checker exactly one square to the right, so the game lasts exactly $2011-3=2008$ moves, whatever Rachel does. The operations commute, so the final configuration depends only on how many times Rachel fights. Each fight adds a white checker, so different numbers of fights give different numbers of white checkers, hence different final configurations. The number of fights can be any of $0,1,\dots,2008$, so there are $2009$ final configurations.

**Answer: 2009**

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ be a set of positive integers such that $a_1=2$ and $a_m=\phi(a_{m+1})$ for all $1\le m\le n-1$, where, for all positive integers $k$, $\phi(k)$ denotes the number of positive integers less than or equal to $k$ that are relatively prime to $k$. Prove that $a_n\ge2^{n-1}$.

solutions.title: phi(s) is even, and phi(t) <= t/2 for even t
solutions.body:
*Fact 1: if $s>2$ then $\phi(s)$ is even.* Let $A_s=\{x\le s:\gcd(x,s)=1\}$. Since $\gcd(x,s)=\gcd(s-x,s)$, $x\in A_s\iff s-x\in A_s$, and $x\ne s-x$ because $s/2$ is not coprime to $s$ for $s>2$. So $A_s$ splits into pairs and $\phi(s)=|A_s|$ is even.

*Fact 2: if $t$ is even then $\phi(t)\le t/2$.* No even number is coprime to $t$, so $A_t$ consists of odd numbers $\le t$, and there are $t/2$ of those.

Since $\phi(s)<s$ for $s\ge2$, the sequence is increasing, $a_1=2$ and so $a_j>2$ for $j\ge2$. By Fact 1, $a_m=\phi(a_{m+1})$ is even for every $m\le n-1$. For $2\le j\le n-1$, $a_j$ is even, so Fact 2 gives $a_{j-1}=\phi(a_j)\le a_j/2$, i.e. $a_j\ge2a_{j-1}$. Hence $a_{n-1}\ge2^{n-2}a_1=2^{n-1}$ (for $n\ge2$), and since $a_n>a_{n-1}$ (because $\phi(a_n)=a_{n-1}<a_n$), $a_n\ge2^{n-1}$. For $n=1$ the claim reads $2\ge1$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be complex numbers such that $|a|=|b|=|c|=|a+b+c|=1$. If $|a-b|=|a-c|$ and $b\ne c$, prove that $|a+b||a+c|=2$.

solutions.title: Normalise a = 1
solutions.body:
Put $u=b/a$, $v=c/a$ (note $a\ne0$). Dividing everything by $|a|=1$ gives $|u|=|v|=|1+u+v|=1$, $|1-u|=|1-v|$, $u\ne v$, and we must show $|1+u||1+v|=2$.

Squaring $|1-u|=|1-v|$: $2-2\operatorname{Re}u=2-2\operatorname{Re}v$, so $\operatorname{Re}u=\operatorname{Re}v$. Two points on the unit circle with equal real part are equal or conjugate; as $u\ne v$, $v=\bar u$. Then $1=|1+u+\bar u|=|1+2\operatorname{Re}u|$, so $\operatorname{Re}u\in\{0,-1\}$. If $\operatorname{Re}u=-1$ then $u=-1=\bar u=v$, a contradiction. So $\operatorname{Re}u=0$, $u=\pm i$, $v=\mp i$, and
$$|1+u||1+v|=|1+i||1-i|=\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2=2 .$$
$\blacksquare$

prompt: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. Define two sequences of real numbers $\{a_n\}$ and $\{b_n\}$ for all positive integers $n$ by $(a+bi)^n=a_n+b_ni$. Prove that $$\frac{|a_{n+1}|+|b_{n+1}|}{|a_n|+|b_n|}\ge\frac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}$$ for all positive integers $n$.
answer: Proof of the inequality (triangle inequality on $z^{n}\pm\bar z^{n}$).

solutions.title: Rewrite with z and its conjugate
solutions.body:
Let $z=a+bi$. Then $a_n=\frac{z^n+\bar z^n}2$, $b_n=\frac{z^n-\bar z^n}{2i}$, so
$$|a_n|+|b_n|=\tfrac12\bigl(|z^n+\bar z^n|+|z^n-\bar z^n|\bigr),$$
and, since $a,b>0$, $\dfrac{a^2+b^2}{a+b}=\dfrac{2z\bar z}{|z+\bar z|+|z-\bar z|}$. Clearing denominators (all positive), the claim is equivalent to
$$\bigl(|z^{n+1}+\bar z^{n+1}|+|z^{n+1}-\bar z^{n+1}|\bigr)\bigl(|z+\bar z|+|z-\bar z|\bigr)\ge2z\bar z\bigl(|z^n+\bar z^n|+|z^n-\bar z^n|\bigr).$$
Expand the left side using $|u||v|=|uv|$ into four terms. Put
$$A=z^{n+2}+\bar z^{n+2},\quad B=z^{n+1}\bar z+z\bar z^{n+1},\quad A'=z^{n+2}-\bar z^{n+2},\quad B'=z^{n+1}\bar z-z\bar z^{n+1}.$$
Then
$$(z^{n+1}+\bar z^{n+1})(z+\bar z)=A+B,\qquad(z^{n+1}-\bar z^{n+1})(z-\bar z)=A-B,$$
$$(z^{n+1}+\bar z^{n+1})(z-\bar z)=A'-B',\qquad(z^{n+1}-\bar z^{n+1})(z+\bar z)=A'+B'.$$
So the left side is $|A+B|+|A-B|+|A'-B'|+|A'+B'|$. By the triangle inequality $|A+B|+|A-B|\ge2|B|$ and $|A'-B'|+|A'+B'|\ge2|B'|$. Since $z\bar z>0$ is real, $2z\bar z|z^n+\bar z^n|=2|B|$ and $2z\bar z|z^n-\bar z^n|=2|B'|$, so the left side is at least the right side. $\blacksquare$

prompt: In a one-player game, the player begins with $4m$ fair coins. On each of $m$ turns, the player takes $4$ unused coins, flips $3$ of them randomly to heads or tails, and then selects whether the $4$th one is heads or tails (these four coins are then considered used). After $m$ turns, when the sides of all $4m$ coins have been determined, if half the coins are heads and half are tails, the player wins; otherwise, the player loses. Prove that whenever the player must choose the side of a coin, the optimal strategy is to choose heads if more coins have been determined tails than heads and to choose tails if more coins have been determined heads than tails.
answer: Proof by induction on the number of turns left.

solutions.title: Induction on the number of remaining turns
solutions.body:
After each complete turn $H-T$ is even. Let $q_n(k)$ be the winning probability under optimal play when $n$ turns remain and $|H-T|=k$ ($k$ even, $k\ge0$); by symmetry it depends only on $|H-T|$. We prove by induction on $n$:

($\ast$) $q_n(k)\ge q_n(k+2)$ for all even $k\ge0$, and with $n$ turns left the optimal choice of the fourth coin minimises $|H-T|$.

*Base $n=0$:* $q_0(0)=1$ and $q_0(k)=0$ for $k>0$, so ($\ast$) holds.

*Step.* Let $D=H-T$ at the start of a turn with $n$ turns left. The three random coins change $D$ by $\delta=2h-3$, where $h\sim\mathrm{Bin}(3,\tfrac12)$: $\delta=-3,-1,1,3$ with probabilities $\tfrac18,\tfrac38,\tfrac38,\tfrac18$. Then $x=D+\delta$ is odd and the fourth coin gives $x\pm1$; with $n-1$ turns left the winning chance is $q_{n-1}(|x\pm1|)$. By the induction hypothesis $q_{n-1}$ is non-increasing in $|\cdot|$, so the optimal choice minimises $|x\pm1|$, i.e. it moves $|H-T|$ towards $0$: choose heads if $x<0$ (more tails than heads) and tails if $x>0$. This is the claimed strategy.

It remains to show $q_n(k)\ge q_n(k+2)$. With the strategy just found, for $k=|D|$:
$$q_n(0)=\tfrac34q_{n-1}(0)+\tfrac14q_{n-1}(2),\qquad q_n(2)=\tfrac12q_{n-1}(0)+\tfrac38q_{n-1}(2)+\tfrac18q_{n-1}(4),$$
$$q_n(4)=\tfrac18q_{n-1}(0)+\tfrac38q_{n-1}(2)+\tfrac38q_{n-1}(4)+\tfrac18q_{n-1}(6),$$
and for $k\ge4$: $q_n(k)=\tfrac18q_{n-1}(k-4)+\tfrac38q_{n-1}(k-2)+\tfrac38q_{n-1}(k)+\tfrac18q_{n-1}(k+2)$. For $k\ge4$ the inequality $q_n(k)\ge q_n(k+2)$ follows termwise from the induction hypothesis. For the first two cases, using $q_{n-1}(2),q_{n-1}(4),q_{n-1}(6)\le q_{n-1}(0)$:
$$q_n(0)-q_n(2)=\tfrac14q_{n-1}(0)-\tfrac18q_{n-1}(2)-\tfrac18q_{n-1}(4)\ge0,$$
$$q_n(2)-q_n(4)=\tfrac38q_{n-1}(0)-\tfrac14q_{n-1}(4)-\tfrac18q_{n-1}(6)\ge0 .$$
This completes the induction and the proof. $\blacksquare$

prompt: In a one-player game, the player begins with $4m$ fair coins. On each of $m$ turns, the player takes $4$ unused coins, flips $3$ of them randomly to heads or tails, and then selects whether the $4$th one is heads or tails (these four coins are then considered used). After $m$ turns, when the sides of all $4m$ coins have been determined, if half the coins are heads and half are tails, the player wins; otherwise, the player loses. Let $T$ denote the number of coins determined tails and $H$ the number determined heads at the end of the game. Let $p_m(k)$ be the probability that $|T-H|=k$ after a game with $4m$ coins, assuming that the player follows the optimal strategy that, whenever the player must choose the side of a coin, chooses heads if more coins have been determined tails than heads and tails if more coins have been determined heads than tails. Clearly $p_m(k)=0$ if $k$ is odd. By definition $p_0(0)=1$ and $p_0(k)=0$ for $k\ge1$. Prove that $p_m(0)\ge p_{m+1}(0)$ for all nonnegative integers $m$.

solutions.title: Compare with the winning probability
solutions.body:
Let $q_n(k)$ be the winning probability with $n$ turns left and $|H-T|=k$, under the optimal strategy (this is the strategy in the statement; see the previous problem for the fact that $q_n(k)\ge q_n(k+2)$). Starting from $0$, the chance that the game ends with $|T-H|=0$ is exactly the chance of winning, so $p_n(0)=q_n(0)$.

From $|H-T|=0$ with $n+1$ turns left: with probability $\tfrac34$ the first turn leaves $|H-T|=0$ and with probability $\tfrac14$ it leaves $|H-T|=2$. Hence
$$q_{n+1}(0)=\tfrac34q_n(0)+\tfrac14q_n(2)\le q_n(0),$$
because $q_n(2)\le q_n(0)$. Therefore $p_{n+1}(0)\le p_n(0)$. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Coupling argument
solutions.body: In a game with $n+1$ turns, after the first turn $|H-T|=0$ with probability $\tfrac34$ and $2$ with probability $\tfrac14$. Suppose the first three coins show two tails and one head (so $H-T=-1$). Compare two strategies for the rest: A: choose the fourth coin heads, then play optimally; the winning chance is $p_n(0)$. B: choose the fourth coin heads with probability $\tfrac34$ and tails with probability $\tfrac14$, then play optimally; this is the same as re-flipping the first three coins, so its winning chance is $p_{n+1}(0)$. Strategy A is optimal at that point, so $p_{n+1}(0)\le p_n(0)$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: In a one-player game, the player begins with $4m$ fair coins. On each of $m$ turns, the player takes $4$ unused coins, flips $3$ of them randomly to heads or tails, and then selects whether the $4$th one is heads or tails (these four coins are then considered used). After $m$ turns, when the sides of all $4m$ coins have been determined, if half the coins are heads and half are tails, the player wins; otherwise, the player loses. Let $T$ denote the number of coins determined tails and $H$ the number determined heads at the end of the game. Let $p_m(k)$ be the probability that $|T-H|=k$ after a game with $4m$ coins, assuming that the player follows the optimal strategy that, whenever the player must choose the side of a coin, chooses heads if more coins have been determined tails than heads and tails if more coins have been determined heads than tails. Clearly $p_m(k)=0$ if $k$ is odd. By definition $p_0(0)=1$ and $p_0(k)=0$ for $k\ge1$. Find $a_1$, $a_2$, and $a_3$ so that the following equation holds for all $m\ge1$: $$p_m(0)=a_1p_{m-1}(0)+a_2p_{m-1}(2)+a_3p_{m-1}(4).$$

solutions.title: Condition on the last turn
solutions.body:
Under the optimal strategy $|H-T|$ is a Markov chain with one step per turn. Condition on the state after $m-1$ turns and look at the last turn. From $|H-T|=j$ the three random coins change $H-T$ by $\delta\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}$ with probabilities $\tfrac18,\tfrac38,\tfrac38,\tfrac18$; the fourth coin then moves the (odd) value $x=j+\delta$ toward $0$ to $|x|-1$.

- From $j=0$: $|x|\in\{3,1,1,3\}$, final $|H-T|=0$ with probability $\tfrac34$ and $2$ with probability $\tfrac14$.
- From $j=2$: $x\in\{-1,1,3,5\}$ with probabilities $\tfrac18,\tfrac38,\tfrac38,\tfrac18$, final $0,0,2,4$: to $0$ with probability $\tfrac12$.
- From $j=4$: $x\in\{1,3,5,7\}$, final $0,2,4,6$: to $0$ with probability $\tfrac18$.
- From $j\ge6$ the final value is at least $2$.

So $p_m(0)=\tfrac34p_{m-1}(0)+\tfrac12p_{m-1}(2)+\tfrac18p_{m-1}(4)$.

**Answer: $a_1=\tfrac34$, $a_2=\tfrac12$, $a_3=\tfrac18$**

prompt: In a one-player game, the player begins with $4m$ fair coins. On each of $m$ turns, the player takes $4$ unused coins, flips $3$ of them randomly to heads or tails, and then selects whether the $4$th one is heads or tails (these four coins are then considered used). After $m$ turns, when the sides of all $4m$ coins have been determined, if half the coins are heads and half are tails, the player wins; otherwise, the player loses. Let $T$ denote the number of coins determined tails and $H$ the number determined heads at the end of the game. Let $p_m(k)$ be the probability that $|T-H|=k$ after a game with $4m$ coins, assuming that the player follows the optimal strategy that, whenever the player must choose the side of a coin, chooses heads if more coins have been determined tails than heads and tails if more coins have been determined heads than tails. Clearly $p_m(k)=0$ if $k$ is odd. By definition $p_0(0)=1$ and $p_0(k)=0$ for $k\ge1$. Find $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$, and $c_4$ so that the following equation holds for all $m\ge1$ and $j\ge2$: $$p_m(2j)=c_1p_{m-1}(2j-2)+c_2p_{m-1}(2j)+c_3p_{m-1}(2j+2)+c_4p_{m-1}(2j+4).$$

solutions.title: Binomial weights
solutions.body:
For $j\ge2$, ending at $|H-T|=2j$ means $x=j'+\delta$ with $|x|-1=2j$, i.e. $x=2j+1$, from a previous value $j'=2j+1-\delta$: $j'=2j-2$ ($\delta=3$, probability $\tfrac18$), $2j$ ($\delta=1$, $\tfrac38$), $2j+2$ ($\delta=-1$, $\tfrac38$), $2j+4$ ($\delta=-3$, $\tfrac18$). (No contribution from $x=-(2j+1)$ because all these previous values are $\ge2$ and $\delta\ge-3$ keep $x>0$.) So $p_m(2j)=\tfrac18p_{m-1}(2j-2)+\tfrac38p_{m-1}(2j)+\tfrac38p_{m-1}(2j+2)+\tfrac18p_{m-1}(2j+4)$.

**Answer: $c_1=\tfrac18$, $c_2=\tfrac38$, $c_3=\tfrac38$, $c_4=\tfrac18$**

prompt: In a one-player game, the player begins with $4m$ fair coins. On each of $m$ turns, the player takes $4$ unused coins, flips $3$ of them randomly to heads or tails, and then selects whether the $4$th one is heads or tails (these four coins are then considered used). After $m$ turns, when the sides of all $4m$ coins have been determined, if half the coins are heads and half are tails, the player wins; otherwise, the player loses. Let $T$ denote the number of coins determined tails and $H$ the number determined heads at the end of the game. Let $p_m(k)$ be the probability that $|T-H|=k$ after a game with $4m$ coins, assuming that the player follows the optimal strategy that, whenever the player must choose the side of a coin, chooses heads if more coins have been determined tails than heads and tails if more coins have been determined heads than tails. Clearly $p_m(k)=0$ if $k$ is odd. By definition $p_0(0)=1$ and $p_0(k)=0$ for $k\ge1$. Using the recurrences $p_m(0)=\tfrac34p_{m-1}(0)+\tfrac12p_{m-1}(2)+\tfrac18p_{m-1}(4)$, $p_m(2)=\tfrac14p_{m-1}(0)+\tfrac38p_{m-1}(2)+\tfrac38p_{m-1}(4)+\tfrac18p_{m-1}(6)$ and, for $j\ge2$, $p_m(2j)=\tfrac18p_{m-1}(2j-2)+\tfrac38p_{m-1}(2j)+\tfrac38p_{m-1}(2j+2)+\tfrac18p_{m-1}(2j+4)$, prove that $\tfrac23p_m(k)\ge p_m(k+2)$ for all $m$ and all even $k\ge0$.

solutions.title: Induction on m
solutions.body:
Write $p=p_n$. For $m=0$ the claim holds ($p_0(0)=1$, other values $0$). Assume $p_n(k+2)\le\tfrac23p_n(k)$ for all even $k$; then also $p_n(2i)\le(\tfrac23)^ip_n(0)$. We show the claim for $n+1$.

*$k\ge4$* (so that $k$ and $k+2$ both use the last recurrence): termwise,
$$p_{n+1}(k+2)=\tfrac18p(k)+\tfrac38p(k+2)+\tfrac38p(k+4)+\tfrac18p(k+6)\le\tfrac23\Bigl[\tfrac18p(k-2)+\tfrac38p(k)+\tfrac38p(k+2)+\tfrac18p(k+4)\Bigr]=\tfrac23p_{n+1}(k).$$

*$k=2$:*
$$\tfrac23p_{n+1}(2)-p_{n+1}(4)=\tfrac16p(0)+\tfrac18p(2)-\tfrac18p(4)-\tfrac7{24}p(6)-\tfrac18p(8).$$
Since $\tfrac18(p(2)-p(4))\ge0$, $p(6)\le\tfrac8{27}p(0)$, $p(8)\le\tfrac{16}{81}p(0)$, this is at least $\bigl(\tfrac16-\tfrac7{81}-\tfrac2{81}\bigr)p(0)=\tfrac1{18}p(0)>0$.

*$k=0$:*
$$\tfrac23p_{n+1}(0)-p_{n+1}(2)=\tfrac14p(0)-\tfrac1{24}p(2)-\tfrac7{24}p(4)-\tfrac18p(6)\ge\Bigl(\tfrac14-\tfrac1{36}-\tfrac7{54}-\tfrac1{27}\Bigr)p(0)=\tfrac1{18}p(0)>0 .$$
This completes the induction. $\blacksquare$

prompt: In a one-player game, the player begins with $4m$ fair coins. On each of $m$ turns, the player takes $4$ unused coins, flips $3$ of them randomly to heads or tails, and then selects whether the $4$th one is heads or tails (these four coins are then considered used). After $m$ turns, when the sides of all $4m$ coins have been determined, if half the coins are heads and half are tails, the player wins; otherwise, the player loses. Let $T$ denote the number of coins determined tails and $H$ the number determined heads at the end of the game. Let $p_m(k)$ be the probability that $|T-H|=k$ after a game with $4m$ coins, assuming that the player follows the optimal strategy that, whenever the player must choose the side of a coin, chooses heads if more coins have been determined tails than heads and tails if more coins have been determined heads than tails. Clearly $p_m(k)=0$ if $k$ is odd. By definition $p_0(0)=1$ and $p_0(k)=0$ for $k\ge1$. Prove that $A_0=\lim_{m\to\infty}p_m(0)$ exists and that $A_0>0$. (You may use that a non-increasing sequence of real numbers that is bounded below by a constant $c$ converges to a limit that is at least $c$. You may also use $p_m(0)\ge p_{m+1}(0)$ and $\tfrac23p_m(k)\ge p_m(k+2)$ for all $m$ and even $k$.)

solutions.title: Monotone and bounded below
solutions.body:
From $\tfrac23p_m(k)\ge p_m(k+2)$ we get $p_m(2i)\le(\tfrac23)^ip_m(0)$. The probabilities sum to $1$, so
$$1=\sum_{i\ge0}p_m(2i)\le p_m(0)\sum_{i\ge0}\left(\tfrac23\right)^i=3p_m(0),$$
hence $p_m(0)\ge\tfrac13$ for all $m$. The sequence $p_m(0)$ is non-increasing and bounded below by $\tfrac13$, so it converges to a limit $A_0\ge\tfrac13>0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: In a one-player game, the player begins with $4m$ fair coins. On each of $m$ turns, the player takes $4$ unused coins, flips $3$ of them randomly to heads or tails, and then selects whether the $4$th one is heads or tails (these four coins are then considered used). After $m$ turns, when the sides of all $4m$ coins have been determined, if half the coins are heads and half are tails, the player wins; otherwise, the player loses. Let $T$ denote the number of coins determined tails and $H$ the number determined heads at the end of the game. Let $p_m(k)$ be the probability that $|T-H|=k$ after a game with $4m$ coins, assuming that the player follows the optimal strategy that, whenever the player must choose the side of a coin, chooses heads if more coins have been determined tails than heads and tails if more coins have been determined heads than tails. Clearly $p_m(k)=0$ if $k$ is odd. By definition $p_0(0)=1$ and $p_0(k)=0$ for $k\ge1$. Assume that the limits $A_k=\lim_{m\to\infty}p_m(k)$ exist, that $A_k\ge0$, that $\sum_{k\ge0}A_{2k}=1$, and that $A_0=\tfrac34A_0+\tfrac12A_2+\tfrac18A_4$, $A_2=\tfrac14A_0+\tfrac38A_2+\tfrac38A_4+\tfrac18A_6$, $A_{2j}=\tfrac18A_{2j-2}+\tfrac38A_{2j}+\tfrac38A_{2j+2}+\tfrac18A_{2j+4}$ for $j\ge2$. Determine, with proof, the value of $A_0$.

solutions.title: Solve the linear recurrence
solutions.body:
Let $B_j=A_{2j}$. For $j\ge2$ the last relation reads $5B_j=B_{j-1}+3B_{j+1}+B_{j+2}$. Its characteristic equation is $x^3+3x^2-5x+1=0$, i.e. $(x-1)(x^2+4x-1)=0$, with roots $1$, $r=\sqrt5-2$ and $s=-2-\sqrt5$. So for $j\ge1$, $B_j=\alpha+\beta r^j+\gamma s^j$. Since $\sum B_j$ converges, $B_j\to0$, which forces $\alpha=\gamma=0$ (because $|s|>1$). Hence $B_j=\beta r^j$ for $j\ge1$.

The relation for $A_0$ gives $A_0=2A_2+\tfrac12A_4=\beta\left(2r+\tfrac{r^2}2\right)$. With $r=\sqrt5-2$, $r^2=9-4\sqrt5$: $2r+\tfrac{r^2}{2}=2\sqrt5-4+\tfrac92-2\sqrt5=\tfrac12$, so $A_0=\tfrac\beta2$.

The total probability: $1=A_0+\sum_{j\ge1}\beta r^j=\tfrac\beta2+\beta\frac r{1-r}$. Since $\dfrac r{1-r}=\dfrac{\sqrt5-2}{3-\sqrt5}=\dfrac{(\sqrt5-2)(3+\sqrt5)}4=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}4$, we get $1=\beta\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt5+1}{4}$, so $\beta=\sqrt5-1$ and
$$A_0=\frac{\sqrt5-1}2 .$$
(One checks that the remaining relation for $A_2$ is then consistent.)

**Answer: $A_0=\dfrac{\sqrt5-1}2$**

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a non-isosceles, non-right triangle, let $\omega$ be its circumcircle, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $BC$. Let the circumcircle of triangle $AOM$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$. If $H$ is the orthocenter of triangle $ABC$, prove that $\angle DAH=\angle MAO$.

solutions.title: Pole of BC and similar triangles
solutions.body:
Let $X$ be the intersection of the tangents to $\omega$ at $B$ and $C$ (they meet since $\angle A\ne90^\circ$, so $BC$ is not a diameter). Then $O,M,X$ are collinear, with $OM\perp BC$. The right triangles $OMC$ (right angle at $M$) and $OCX$ (right angle at $C$) share the angle at $O$, so they are similar and $\dfrac{OM}{OC}=\dfrac{OC}{OX}$. As $OC=OA$, this reads $\dfrac{OM}{OA}=\dfrac{OA}{OX}$; together with the common angle $\angle MOA=\angle AOX$, SAS gives
$$\triangle OAM\sim\triangle OXA,\qquad\text{so}\quad\angle OAM=\angle OXA\ \text{ and }\ \angle OMA=\angle OAX .$$
Since $A,O,M,D$ are concyclic, $\angle OMA=\angle ODA$; as $OA=OD$, $\angle ODA=\angle OAD$. Hence $\angle OAX=\angle OAD$, i.e. $A$, $D$, $X$ are collinear.

Finally $AH\perp BC$ and $OX\perp BC$, so $AH\parallel OX$ and $\angle DAH=\angle AXO$ (alternate angles along line $AX$). Therefore $\angle DAH=\angle OXA=\angle OAM=\angle MAO$. (Using directed angles makes this valid in every configuration.) $\blacksquare$

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $E$ and $F$ be the feet of the altitudes from $B$ and $C$, respectively. If $A$ is not a right angle, prove that the circumcenter of triangle $AEF$ lies on the incircle of triangle $ABC$ if and only if the incenter of triangle $ABC$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $AEF$.
answer: Proof: both conditions are equivalent to $2\sin\frac A2\cos\frac{B-C}2=1$.

solutions.title: Reduce both conditions to one trigonometric equation
solutions.body:
Let $R,r$ be the circumradius and inradius, $H$ the orthocenter, $I$ the incenter, and write $s=\sin\frac A2$, $c=\cos\frac{B-C}2$, $k=\cos A$. Since $\angle AEH=\angle AFH=90^\circ$, the circle $AEF$ has diameter $AH$: its circumcenter is the midpoint $M$ of $AH$ and its radius is $MA=\tfrac12AH$. (This also holds when $A$ is obtuse.)

*Standard facts.* $AH=2R\cos A$ measured along the altitude $AD$ from $A$ toward $BC$ (signed: negative for obtuse $A$); $AI=\dfrac r{\sin(A/2)}=4R\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2=2R(c-s)$, using $2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2=\cos\frac{B-C}2-\cos\frac{B+C}2=c-s$; and the angle between the bisector $AI$ and the altitude $AD$ is $\left|\frac{B-C}2\right|$, whose cosine is $c$. Note $c>s>0$.

By the law of cosines in triangle $AMI$ (with signed $AM=R\,k$),
$$MI^2=R^2k^2+AI^2-2Rk\,AI\cdot c .$$

**(1) $I$ lies on circle $AEF$ iff $MI=MA$.**
$$MI^2-MA^2=AI\,(AI-2Rkc)=2R(c-s)\cdot2R\bigl(c-s-kc\bigr).$$
With $k=1-2s^2$, $c-s-kc=2s^2c-s=s(2sc-1)$, so $MI^2-MA^2=4R^2s(c-s)(2sc-1)$, which vanishes iff $2sc=1$.

**(2) $M$ lies on the incircle iff $MI=r$.** Here $r=AI\cdot s=2R(c-s)s$. Then
$$MI^2-r^2=R^2\Bigl[k^2-4kc(c-s)+4(1-s^2)(c-s)^2\Bigr].$$
Substituting $k=1-2s^2$ and collecting powers of $c$: the coefficient of $c^2$ is $-4(1-2s^2)+4(1-s^2)=4s^2$, of $c$ is $4s(1-2s^2)-8s(1-s^2)=-4s$, and the constant is $(1-2s^2)^2+4s^2(1-s^2)=1$. So
$$MI^2-r^2=R^2\bigl(4s^2c^2-4sc+1\bigr)=R^2(2sc-1)^2,$$
which vanishes iff $2sc=1$.

Thus both statements are equivalent to $2\sin\frac A2\cos\frac{B-C}2=1$, and hence to each other. $\blacksquare$

(The two identities were also checked numerically on random triangles.)

prompt: Given positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $a>b$, define a sequence of ordered pairs $(a_l,b_l)$ for nonnegative integers $l$ by $a_0=a$, $b_0=b$, and $(a_{l+1},b_{l+1})=(b_l,\ a_l\bmod b_l)$, where, for all positive integers $x$ and $y$, $x\bmod y$ is the remainder left by $x$ upon division by $y$. Define $f(a,b)$ to be the smallest positive integer $j$ such that $b_j=0$. Given a positive integer $n$, define $g(n)$ to be $\max_{1\le k\le n-1}f(n,k)$. Given a positive integer $m$, what is the smallest positive integer $n_m$ such that $g(n_m)=m$?

solutions.title: Fibonacci lower bound
solutions.body:
Let $F_0=1$, $F_1=1$, $F_2=2$, $F_{i+1}=F_i+F_{i-1}$. 

*Claim.* If $a>b\ge1$ and $f(a,b)=m$, then $a\ge F_{m+1}$ and $b\ge F_m$.

For $m=1$: $b\mid a$ and $a>b$, so $a\ge2=F_2$, $b\ge1=F_1$. For $m\ge2$: $(b,c)$ with $c=a\bmod b$ satisfies $b>c\ge1$ and $f(b,c)=m-1$, so by induction $b\ge F_m$ and $c\ge F_{m-1}$; then $a=qb+c\ge b+c\ge F_m+F_{m-1}=F_{m+1}$.

Consequently, if $g(n)=m$ there is a $k$ with $f(n,k)=m$, so $n\ge F_{m+1}$. Conversely $f(F_{m+1},F_m)=m$ (the Euclidean algorithm on consecutive Fibonacci numbers removes one index per step, ending $(2,1)\to(1,0)$), and no $k$ has $f(F_{m+1},k)>m$, since that would force $F_{m+1}\ge F_{m+2}$. So $g(F_{m+1})=m$ and $n_m=F_{m+1}$. (Check: $n_1=2$, $n_2=3$, $n_3=5$, $n_4=8$.)

**Answer: $n_m=F_{m+1}$ with $F_1=1$, $F_2=2$**

prompt: Given positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $a>b$, define a sequence of ordered pairs $(a_l,b_l)$ for nonnegative integers $l$ by $a_0=a$, $b_0=b$, and $(a_{l+1},b_{l+1})=(b_l,\ a_l\bmod b_l)$. Define $f(a,b)$ to be the smallest positive integer $j$ such that $b_j=0$, and for a positive integer $n$ define $g(n)=\max_{1\le k\le n-1}f(n,k)$. Given a positive integer $m$, what is the second smallest positive integer $n$ such that $g(n)=m$?
answer: For $m\ge2$ it is $F_{m+1}+F_{m-1}$, i.e. $L_{m+1}$ with $L_1=1,\ L_2=3,\ L_{i+1}=L_i+L_{i-1}$ (no second smallest exists for $m=1$).

solutions.title: Continuants
solutions.body:
Use $F_0=F_1=1$, $F_2=2$, $F_{i+1}=F_i+F_{i-1}$ and let $S_m=\{n:g(n)=m\}$, $A_m=\{n:\exists k,\ f(n,k)=m\}\supseteq S_m$.

For $m=1$, $g(n)=1$ only for $n=2$ (all of $1,\dots,n-1$ must divide $n$), so there is no second smallest. Let $m\ge2$.

If $f(a,b)=m$, let $q_1,\dots,q_m$ be the quotients in the Euclidean algorithm ($q_i\ge1$, $q_m\ge2$) and $d=\gcd(a,b)$. Then $a=d\,K(q_1,\dots,q_m)$, where the continuant $K$ (numerator of the continued fraction $[q_1;q_2,\dots,q_m]$, with $K(\varnothing)=1$) is increasing in each argument and linear in $q_i$ with slope $K(q_1,\dots,q_{i-1})K(q_{i+1},\dots,q_m)$. The smallest value is $K(1,\dots,1,2)=F_{m+1}$ (consistent with part (a)).

Any other admissible sequence $q\ne q^*=(1,\dots,1,2)$ has some $q_i\ge q^*_i+1$, so by monotonicity $K(q)\ge K(q^*+e_i)$, where $q^*+e_i$ raises the $i$th entry by $1$. Also $d\ge2$ gives $dK\ge2F_{m+1}>F_{m+1}+F_{m-1}$. So the second smallest element of $A_m$ is $F_{m+1}+\min_i\mathrm{slope}_i$ with
$$\mathrm{slope}_i=F_{i-1}F_{m-i+1}\ (1\le i\le m-1),\qquad\mathrm{slope}_m=F_{m-1}$$
(using $K(1^j)=F_j$ and $K(1^j,2)=F_{j+2}$). For $1\le i\le m-1$ put $u=i-1$, $v=m-i+1\ge2$: $F_uF_v\ge F_{u+v-1}=F_{m-1}$, because splitting a tiling of a board of length $u+v-1$ by squares and dominoes at position $u$ gives $F_{u+v-1}=F_uF_{v-1}+F_{u-1}F_{v-2}\le F_uF_{v-1}+F_uF_{v-2}=F_uF_v$ (for $u=0$ it reads $F_m\ge F_{m-1}$). So the minimum slope is $F_{m-1}$ and the second smallest element of $A_m$ is $F_{m+1}+F_{m-1}$.

This number lies in $S_m$: it is $<F_{m+2}=F_{m+1}+F_m$, so by the claim of part (a) no $k$ gives $f>m$, and it is in $A_m$. Since $F_{m+1}\in S_m$ too, the second smallest element of $S_m$ is $F_{m+1}+F_{m-1}$. This is $L_{m+1}$ (e.g. $4,7,11,18,29,\dots$ for $m=2,3,4,5,6$; a computer check of $g(n)$ for $n<2000$ agrees).

**Answer: $F_{m+1}+F_{m-1}$ ($=L_{m+1}$) for $m\ge2$**

prompt: Given a positive integer $n$, a sequence of integers $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_r$, where $0\le a_i\le k$ for all $1\le i\le r$, is said to be a ``$k$-representation'' of $n$ if there exists an integer $c$ such that $$\sum_{i=1}^ra_i=\sum_{i=1}^ra_ik^{c-i}=n.$$ Prove that every positive integer $n$ has a $k$-representation, and that the $k$-representation is unique if and only if $0$ does not appear in the base-$k$ representation of $n-1$. (Here $k\ge2$ is an integer; representations that differ only by zeros at the ends are regarded as the same.)
answer: Proof (existence; uniqueness iff no digit $0$ in $n-1$, apart from the exceptional case $n=k+1$).

solutions.title: Digits indexed by exponent
solutions.body:
Index digits by the exponent $e=c-i$. A $k$-representation of $n$ is then a finitely supported digit sequence $(d_e)_{e\in\mathbb Z}$ with $0\le d_e\le k$ and
$$\sum_ed_e=\sum_ed_ek^e=n .$$

**Existence.** Let $n-1=\sum_{i=0}^r\alpha_ik^i$ be any expression with digits $0\le\alpha_i\le k$ (e.g. base $k$).
- If $\alpha_i=0$ for all $i\ge1$ then $n\le k$ and $d_0=n$ works.
- Otherwise let $l=\sum_{i\ge1}\alpha_i(k^{i-1}+\dots+1)\ge1$ and put $d_e=\alpha_e$ ($0\le e\le r$), $d_e=k-1$ for $-l<e<0$, $d_{-l}=k$. Then $\sum d_ek^e=(n-1)+(1-k^{1-l})+k^{1-l}=n$, and $\sum d_e=\sum\alpha_i+(l-1)(k-1)+k=\sum\alpha_i+\sum_{i\ge1}\alpha_i(k^i-1)+1=n$.

**Non-uniqueness if $0$ occurs (and $n\ne k+1$).** Let $\alpha_i$ be the base-$k$ digits of $n-1$ and $i$ the largest index with $\alpha_i=0$ (so $i<r$). Replace $\alpha_i\to k$, $\alpha_{i+1}\to\alpha_{i+1}-1$; this is still an expression of $n-1$ with digits in $[0,k]$, and the construction above gives a second representation (it differs from the first at exponent $i\ge0$). The construction needs that some digit with index $\ge1$ is nonzero, which fails only if $i=0$, $r=1$, $\alpha_1=1$, i.e. $n-1=k$. So for $n=k+1$ this argument breaks down, and indeed the representation is then unique.

**Uniqueness if no digit of $n-1$ is $0$.** Let $a$ be the representation constructed from the base-$k$ digits of $n-1$; its support is an interval $[s,r]$ ($s=-l$) on which all digits are nonzero ($\ge1$), and $a_s=k$ is the only digit equal to $k$. Let $b$ be another representation and $c=a-b$. Then $c_e\in[-k,k]$, $\sum c_e=0$, $\sum c_ek^e=0$.

*Block claim.* The nonzero entries of $c$ form disjoint contiguous blocks (separated by zeros) each of the form $B=(1,1-k,\dots,1-k,-k)$ or $-B$, listed from the highest exponent down (possibly $B=(1,-k)$). Proof: take the highest exponent $q$ with $c_q\ne0$, say $c_q>0$. Then $c_qk^q=-\sum_{e<q}c_ek^e\le k\sum_{e<q}k^e<\frac{k}{k-1}k^q\le2k^q$, so $c_q=1$. Now $k^q+c_{q-1}k^{q-1}+\dots=0$ gives $(k+c_{q-1})k^{q-1}+\dots=0$, and in the same way $k+c_{q-1}\in\{0,1\}$, i.e. $c_{q-1}\in\{-k,1-k\}$. If $c_{q-1}=-k$ the first two terms cancel and the block ends; if $c_{q-1}=1-k$ they add up to $k^{q-1}$ and the same argument repeats from exponent $q-1$. Remove the block and continue.

The sum of the entries of $B$ is $(1-k)(\text{length}-1)<0$, so $\sum c_e=0$ forces blocks of both signs if $c\ne0$.

A block $B$ ($+$): its lowest entry $-k$ means $a_p=0$, $b_p=k$, so $p\notin[s,r]$; its top entry $1$ means $a_q\ge1$, so $q\in[s,r]$; hence $p<s\le q$ and the block contains the position $s$. A block $-B$: its lowest entry is $+k$, so $a_p=k$, hence $p=s$; it contains $s$ too. Two disjoint blocks cannot both contain $s$. So $c=0$ and $b=a$. $\blacksquare$

reviewNote: The statement is false for $n=k+1$: then $n-1=k=(10)_k$ contains a $0$, yet the $k$-representation of $n$ is unique (e.g. $k=2$, $n=3$: the only one is digit $2$ at exponent $-1$ and digit $1$ at exponent $1$; verified by computer for $k=2,3,4$). The solution proves the statement for all $n\ne k+1$ and points out this exception.

prompt: Denote $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ by $[n]$, and let $S$ be the set of all permutations of $[n]$. Call a subset $T$ of $S$ good if every permutation $\sigma$ in $S$ may be written as $t_1t_2$ for elements $t_1$ and $t_2$ of $T$, where the product of two permutations is defined to be their composition. Call a subset $U$ of $S$ extremely good if every permutation $\sigma$ in $S$ may be written as $s^{-1}us$ for elements $s$ of $S$ and $u$ of $U$. Let $\tau$ be the smallest value of $|T|/|S|$ for all good subsets $T$, and let $\upsilon$ be the smallest value of $|U|/|S|$ for all extremely good subsets $U$. Prove that $\sqrt\upsilon\ge\tau$.

solutions.title: Involutions, RSK and Cauchy-Schwarz
solutions.body:
**Step 1: the involutions form a good set.** Let $s\in S$ have disjoint cycles $(a_1\,a_2\dots a_l)$ (including fixed points as $1$-cycles). Define $q(a_j)=a_{l+1-j}$ and $r(a_1)=a_1$, $r(a_k)=a_{l+2-k}$ ($k\ge2$) on each cycle (identity elsewhere). Then $q^2=r^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $rq=s$: for $j<l$, $q(a_j)=a_{l+1-j}$ with $l+1-j\ge2$ and $r(a_{l+1-j})=a_{j+1}$; for $j=l$, $q(a_l)=a_1$ and $r(a_1)=a_1$, which is $s(a_l)$. So every permutation is a product of two involutions, and the set $I$ of involutions is good. Hence $\tau\le|I|/n!$.

**Step 2: counting with tableaux.** By the Robinson-Schensted correspondence, permutations of $[n]$ are in bijection with pairs of standard Young tableaux of the same shape $\lambda\vdash n$, and involutions correspond to pairs of *identical* tableaux. With $f^\lambda$ the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$,
$$n!=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}(f^\lambda)^2,\qquad|I|=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}f^\lambda .$$
So $\tau\le\dfrac1{n!}\sum_\lambda f^\lambda$.

**Step 3: a lower bound for $\upsilon$.** Any extremely good $U$ must meet every conjugacy class of $S$. Conjugate permutations have the same cycle type, and every partition of $n$ occurs as a cycle type, so there are at least $p(n)$ conjugacy classes ($p(n)$ the number of partitions of $n$). Hence $|U|\ge p(n)$ and $\upsilon\ge p(n)/n!$.

**Step 4.** By Cauchy-Schwarz,
$$\Bigl(\sum_\lambda f^\lambda\Bigr)^2\le\Bigl(\sum_\lambda(f^\lambda)^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_\lambda1\Bigr)=n!\,p(n)\le n!\cdot\upsilon\,n!,$$
so $\sum_\lambda f^\lambda\le n!\sqrt\upsilon$. Therefore $\tau\le\dfrac{\sum_\lambda f^\lambda}{n!}\le\sqrt\upsilon$. $\blacksquare$
